stories.headline: Officer shot in Thornton, police searching for suspect Luis Arebalo
stories.summary:
Thornton police are searching for a suspect after an officer was shot Sunday night on Ulster Street near East 128th Avenue. The shooting happened around 9:30 p.m. while officers were investigating a report of an unwanted person.

Police say that while officers were speaking with the person who made the report, the suspect fired multiple rounds at them. One officer was struck, and another returned fire. The wounded officer was taken to a hospital with injuries described as serious but not life threatening. It is unclear whether the suspect was hit.

Police identified the suspect early Monday as Luis Arebalo, 37, who fled the scene. He is described as 5-foot-9 and about 180 pounds with brown hair and brown eyes, last seen in a black short-sleeved shirt and dark pants. He is considered armed and dangerous, and the public is urged not to approach him.

Residents nearby were initially told to shelter in place, an order that has since been lifted. Anyone with information can call 911 or Thornton police at 720-977-5069.

stories.headline: Denver Police investigating crash that killed pedestrian
stories.summary:
Denver police are investigating a crash that killed a pedestrian in the city. The department has released limited information about the incident so far.

Details including the location, the time of the crash, the identity of the victim and the circumstances involving the driver have not yet been made public in the available report.

Investigators are expected to release further information as the inquiry continues. Residents with information about the crash are encouraged to contact Denver police.

stories.headline: Therapy dogs bring calm and joy to students at Evergreen High School a year after shooting
stories.summary:
Two golden Labs, Norene and Polenta, now greet students each morning at Evergreen High School as the community continues to heal from a shooting last year. Norene started at the school in March and Polenta in August.

The dogs are part of a program run by Canine Companions, a California-based nonprofit that provides trauma support dogs free of charge. They are the first dogs the group has matched with a school following a shooting on campus.

In September 2025, a 16-year-old student opened fire with a revolver during lunch, wounding two students before shooting himself. The suspect later died. Principal Skyler Artes, who sheltered in the main office with students and staff, trained as a handler after seeing the dogs' impact; she is Norene's handler.

Students say the dogs brighten their days. Last week the pair were crowned prince and princess at the homecoming football game.

stories.headline: Colorado Red Cross volunteers deploy to Gulf Coast after hurricane
stories.summary:
The American Red Cross of Colorado and Wyoming has deployed 16 volunteers to the Gulf Coast to help communities recovering from a major hurricane. Among them are volunteers from Aurora and Silverthorne, who traveled to Florida before landfall.

The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday night, killing at least four people and leaving hundreds of thousands without power. About 485 Red Cross volunteers from across the country have been deployed, and roughly 1,000 people spent Friday night in shelters in Florida, Georgia and Alabama.

Volunteers are staffing shelters, distributing food, water and supplies, and assessing damage. Teams also provide health, mental health and spiritual care.

Coloradans who want to help can donate money, volunteer at RedCross.org/volunteer or schedule a blood donation at RedCrossBlood.org.

stories.headline: Aurora council members ask police to pull Flock cameras from high schools after arrests
stories.summary:
A Denver Gazette editorial defends automated license-plate readers after Aurora officials asked police to remove Flock cameras from five high schools. The request came from the city's recently elected progressive council members.

Aurora police recently arrested four people after a school camera detected a car stolen in a carjacking. The contract is between Flock and the city, so Aurora Public Schools would need its own agreement to keep the cameras. The ACLU and the teachers' union say the cameras threaten student privacy and safety.

The editorial cites Denver's 12-month Flock pilot, during which auto thefts fell from more than 12,000 in 2023 to 8,550, with nearly 300 arrests and 170 vehicles recovered. It notes that Aurora Police Chief Todd Chamberlain and sheriffs Darren Weekly and Tyler Brown praised the technology, while El Paso County's sheriff ended his program over civil liberties concerns.

This item is an opinion piece from the Denver Gazette editorial board.

stories.headline: Colorado ballot carries record-tying 14 statewide measures; Advance Colorado backs six
stories.summary:
Colorado voters face a record-tying 14 statewide initiatives this November, in addition to county, school district and local questions. Thirteen were placed on the ballot by petition and one was referred by the legislature.

Melissa Osse of the Common Sense Institute Colorado said voters are being asked to make decisions that could change the state's tax structure, energy policy, criminal laws, conservation funding and transportation system.

A Gazette column highlights Michael Fields of Advance Colorado, a conservative network backing six measures. They include Proposition 136, capping the state income tax at 4.4 percent, Amendment 81 on notifying federal immigration officials, and Proposition 132 raising fentanyl penalties.

The group also opposes two initiatives that would raise property taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations or let the state keep more tax revenue for schools.

stories.headline: Denver voters to decide five municipal propositions and a DPS tax measure
stories.summary:
Denver voters will see five municipal propositions and a Denver Public Schools tax measure on the Nov. 3 ballot, alongside statewide questions. Topics range from the city budget process to Xcel Energy to foie gras.

One charter amendment would clarify that the Auditor's Office may continue enforcing wage and worker protection laws. The office has collected about $10 million in restitution and enforced the rights of more than 15,000 workers over the past decade. No opposing comments were submitted.

Another would allow a two-year budget cycle, at an estimated $50,000 cost to reconfigure systems. A 2% gap between projected revenues and spending would trigger a public reduction plan, and a 5% gap would require cuts. The city would not be required to adopt a two-year cycle. Opponents question the city's record of forecasting revenue.

The DPS measure is a $44 million tax increase.

stories.headline: Denver Post editorial board opposes Amendment 87 graduated income tax
stories.summary:
The Denver Post editorial board urged voters to reject Amendment 87, which would remove the constitutional ban on a graduated income tax and raise about $2.7 billion in a single year from large businesses.

The board said Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce leader J.J. Ament and Gov. Jared Polis told it that major employers are threatening to leave if the measure passes. Businesses with at least $3 million in taxable profit would see their bills nearly double, while the smallest businesses would see decreases.

The board acknowledged that the flat 4.4% tax burdens the middle class and that education and health care need funding. It also worried lawmakers might use the money for new programs such as universal childcare.

It pointed to Colorado's seven Fortune 500 companies, down from 10 in 2023, as potential departures. This is an opinion piece.

stories.headline: Metro Denver voter guide: in-person voting opens, deadlines for returning ballots
stories.summary:
Election Day is Nov. 3, with polls closing at 7 p.m., and ballots are already in the mail. Every voter will weigh in on the Senate race, while House districts depend on address. Every ballot includes seven propositions and seven amendments.

Denver voters can register until 7 p.m. on Election Day. The Voter Service and Polling Center at the Denver Central Library opens Oct. 12, with other centers opening in phases beginning Oct. 19. The city has 49 centers in total.

Voters can return ballots to one of 43 24-hour drop boxes or to polling centers and drive-throughs. Ballots mailed should be sent by Oct. 26 to arrive in time, and they must be received by Election Day to count.

Voters can track ballots with BallotTrax and request replacements for lost or damaged ballots at 720-913-VOTE.

stories.headline: Broncos beat Chargers 23-17 as defense forces late turnovers
stories.summary:
The Broncos beat the Los Angeles Chargers 23-17 in Inglewood on Sunday, improving to 3-2. Denver's defense forced consecutive takeaways in the fourth quarter after the offense struggled for most of the afternoon.

Zach Allen forced a Justin Herbert fumble on a sack, and Brandon Jones intercepted a fourth-down heave. Ja'Quan McMillian sacked Herbert on the final play. The defense held Los Angeles to 237 yards, a season low, without its top two cornerbacks.

Bo Nix threw for 123 yards, one of the lowest totals of his career, even with Sean Payton back calling plays. Kicker Wil Lutz has missed from 42 and 43 yards in recent weeks. Safety Talanoa Hufanga left late in the third quarter.

Denver next plays Seattle on Thursday night.

stories.headline: Nuggets edge Bulls 133-128 in third preseason game
stories.summary:
The Nuggets held off the Chicago Bulls 133-128 Sunday night at Ball Arena, with Cam Whitmore hitting two free throws with 14 seconds left to clinch the win.

Cam Johnson has looked comfortable in Denver's high-post system, scoring 15 points in the second quarter in 25 minutes. DeMar DeRozan went 0-for-4, and the team was outscored by 10 in his nine first-half minutes as it works to balance his isolation style with other offense.

Marvin Bagley III rested, leaving Zeke Nnaji at backup center. Coach David Adelman is still working out the best lineups around DeRozan.

stories.headline: How Denver became one of the English Premier League's strongest American markets
stories.summary:
Denver has become a hotspot for the English Premier League, as shown by thousands attending the Premier League Mornings Live fan fest at Union Station this weekend. Denver is the 13th city to host the event.

The league's U.S. managing director, Akash Jain, called Denver one of its strongest and fastest-growing American markets. Denver also hosted the Premier League Coast to Coast event focused on Arsenal at McGregor Square in August.

The city has many official supporters clubs, including the Denver Gooners for Arsenal, based at The Celtic, and OLSC Denver for Liverpool, affiliated with The Abbey Tavern. Others support Tottenham, Leeds United, Chelsea and Manchester United.

An estimated 40 million EPL fans live in the U.S., a number boosted by this summer's World Cup.

topStory.headline: Trump Announces Russia-Ukraine 'Energy Ceasefire' as Moscow Stays Silent and Kyiv Says It Learned of It From Media
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday on Truth Social that an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE" between Russia and Ukraine was in effect "immediately," writing that "both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" He gave no details on what the arrangement would cover. Moscow has not confirmed it, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only that "contacts are ongoing" and that Russia would provide information when it had something to say.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the announcement "was news for me" and that Ukraine "learned from the media." He told the Warsaw Security Forum that Kyiv supports the idea but has not heard Russia approve it, calling that "strange." In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's armed forces had received all appropriate orders and that Kyiv was awaiting details of the U.S.-Russia dialogue. He also said he had discussed the proposal with leaders of Canada, Finland and NATO. Ukrainian officials said Russia kept striking energy infrastructure in the hours after Trump's post and on Monday morning, including a power plant or energy facility in and near Kharkiv. CBS News said it had asked the White House for clarification.

The announcement followed several days of tension between Washington and Kyiv. On Friday the United States agreed to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal Trump said would see Russia release 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that. Trump also demanded that Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested Ukraine "get a new leader who can make a deal." Zelenskyy responded that Russia alone is responsible for the war, and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukrainians have the right to choose their leader. Trump made a similar ceasefire announcement about a month ago, and aerial attacks by both sides continued afterward.

Zelenskyy told ABC News' "This Week" that Ukraine is ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and that he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. He disputed Trump's attempt to link high fuel prices to the war in Ukraine, saying the world understands the price increases stem from the war in the Middle East. Trump has blamed the Ukraine conflict rather than the U.S. military campaign against Iran, launched in February, for a global fuel shortage that has pushed diesel prices to record highs. Ukraine continued its long-range campaign on Sunday, with a drone attack shutting down a Yandex data center, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney both voiced support for an energy ceasefire. Burnham said it was "the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets." Carney, however, criticized the U.S.-Russia diesel deal, saying it undermined efforts to ensure stability in Europe and end the war. Whether the ceasefire takes hold depends on whether Russia publicly commits to it and on what terms Washington and Moscow settle. The war has now run more than four and a half years, with the armies largely deadlocked on the front line and both sides relying on long-range strikes.
